title: Backblaze Drive Stats for Q1 2026
summary: Read the Q1 2026 Drive Stats Report to see the latest on failure rates of over 340,000 hard drives.
body_text: Long time readers: I must start with a mea culpa that this article was not released on our traditional May the Fourth (or thereabouts) report date. Please know I missed making the many and sundry Star Wars puns as much as (I’m sure) you missed hearing them—so, I’ll probably slip a few in, just because. That said, there was good reason for the delay. We were diligently investigating a disturbance in the force. (See? We’re back!) We’ll get into the details after we dig into the numbers, but here’s the teaser: this quarter, we observed something unusual in the data that wasn’t entirely a failure trend. It did, however, prompt us to revisit and validate the assumptions behind our Drive Stats analysis before publishing. Sign up for the Drive Stats webinar Ready to dive deeper into the data? Tune in Wednesday, July 15, 2026 at 12:00 noon PT , as Sr. Market Intelligence Manager, Stephanie Doyle, and Sr. Product Marketing Manager, Laquie Campbell review the trends. Join the Webinar Drive Stats: The digest version Q1 2026 Hard drive failure rates As of the end of Q1 2026, Backblaze was monitoring 345,662 drives used to store data. For our evaluation, we removed from consideration 3,907 boot drives and 492 hard drives, as they did not meet the criteria to be included. We’ll discuss the criteria we used in the next section of this report. Removing these drives leaves us with 341,263 hard drives to analyze. The table below shows the annualized failure rates for Q1 2026 for this collection of drives. This is up from last quarter, but down from the previous year. No new drive models this quarter. That’s not unheard of, but it’s pretty rare. In the last eight quarters, we’ve had new drives six times. The investment in higher capacity drives continues. We deployed 10,220 drives last quarter, and 9,404 of those drives had a capacity of more than 20TB. While these drives are still fairly young, their AFR is an impressive 0.85% as a pool. Impressive, most impressive. These drives had zero failures: HGST HMS5C4040BLE640 (4TB) HGST HUH728080ALE600 (8TB) Seagate ST16000NM002J (16TB) And these drives had one: Seagate ST8000NM000A (8TB) Seagate ST12000NM000J (12TB) Seagate ST14000NM000J (14TB) Seagate ST16000NM000J (16TB) Toshiba MG09ACA16TE (16TB) That list proves a point we’ve made in a few different quarters: net failure does not necessarily mean a low AFR. On this list, the Seagate ST16000NM000J (16TB) came in with a 3.61% AFR—when there are only 129 drives left in the fleet, even one failure spikes the AFR. The lifetime failure rate is 1.39%. Hello there! Three drives make their appearance on the lifetime table, including our 26TB drive (which was just under on drive days last time around): Toshiba MG09ACA16TE (16TB) WDC WUH722222ALE6L4 (22TB) WDC WUH722626ALE6L4 (26TB) You served me well. The last of our 4TB drives have finally dropped below the exclusion criteria for the lifetime table. The HGST HMS5C4040ALE640 is completely gone, while the HGST HMS5C4040BLE640 (4TB) has just 186 drives left in the pool. Do or do not: When failure isn’t the only metric in play As I teased in the introduction, this quarter, some unexpected behavior brought forth one of the most interesting edge cases we’ve seen in a while, and it spotlights some relevant truths about the Drive Stats project. More interestingly, it showed up with only slightly higher failure rates, partially because of some mitigation steps we were able to take. Stay with me—there are multiple, overlapping issues at play. We’ve said often that individual drives within a manufacturer pool, and even within a single drive model, can vary quite a bit. On these particular drives, that was the case: there were two different mechanical issues, one which affected writes and one which affected drives when they power cycled. The fact that it was two different types of issues made the initial investigation more difficult, and depending on the age of the drive, either, both, or neither issue could have affected the drive model. Additionally, in both of those types of errors, it didn’t affect every drive in the pool, and for a long period of time, the failure rate was actually acceptable. Once we saw more of the failures happening, we correlated with the power issue, and we could help mitigate by reducing the frequency of the power cycling systems for Vaults that contained these drives. What that looked like in practice is that we put the Vaults with suspected issues into no-upload mode and kept them in reserve. Once the investigation was complete, we were able to understand the full picture. The point I want to highlight here is one that I’ve made quite often: our drive failure rates, and what we report on in general, is the function of people actively managing failure and risk. You can see that clearly here—mitigating one of the two root causes reduced overall risk for this drive model; and, while we were doing that, we had an alternative option that let us use the drives, albeit in a different way. Meanwhile, it also reflects the point we’ve been making from the beginning of time, from way back when we said “why not use consumer hardware to create a storage cloud?” Some level of risk is always acceptable. A system that pushes for absolutely zero failures on the hardware level is imprudent, given that our software layer largely prevents data loss. Always two there are And yet, this investigation was particularly impactful because we saw a decent number of drives (not all of them—again, multiple causes to this incident) that were day one failures. Because that’s true, there’s another important piece of the puzzle to consider, one that speaks to the ways we define a failure and the ways the Drive Stats program is written . The short version is that at the end of each day, a C++ program collects the various SMART stats. If a drive was there the day before and is not there the day of, then it’s logged as a failure. There are other pieces of the puzzle as well, including a lookback period. So if the disappeared drive serial number shows back up on day two (or three or four), it retroactively tells us that it wasn’t a failure. We cut that off at the end of the quarter, which means there’s a handful of drives that might be false positives on that kind of failure, but the probability is quite low (and you have to cut things off somewhere). But the more important part of things is this: Drive Stats is a function of conditional logic. Because it defines a failure based on a drive’s presence in the pool the day before, that means we can’t define day one failures using only the Drive Stats program. What does that mean for us going forward? Have we been completely under-reporting day one failures? Short answer: yes, probably. But, back to that whole “managed environment” caveat—once drives enter data centers, they’ve already gone through a period of drive qualification. So, it’s relatively rare we have day one failures to begin with. But, that does mean that we should caveat things appropriately, particularly if you’re one of the folks who likes to use the full dataset for your projects. The logline data compiles SMART stats, but only for drives that have the chutzpah to make it to the end of day one. Remember the Drive Stats will be with you, always Thank you, as always, for following Drive Stats. We had some folks reach out to make sure the report was going live, particularly because we lost an important member of the team recently, the inimitable Pat Patterson. We appreciate all the well wishes, and the patience. Here’s our standard fine print: The complete dataset used to create the tables and charts in this report is available on our Hard Drive Test Data page . You can download and use this data for free for your own purpose. All we ask are three things: You cite Backblaze as the source if you use the data; You accept that you are solely responsible for how you use the data, and; You do not sell this data itself to anyone; it is free. If you’re a new Drive Stats fan, consider signing up for the newsletter. If you’re not ready for that kind of commitment, sound off in the comments section below or reach out directly to us to let us know what you’re working on. May the Stats be with you!

In addition, Zymeworks is building a portfolio of healthcare assets that can generate strong cash flows, while supporting the development of innovative medicines. title: AWS Lambda now supports Java 8, 11, and 17 on Amazon Linux 2023
summary: Discover more about what's new at AWS with AWS Lambda now supports Java 8, 11, and 17 on Amazon Linux 2023
body_text: AWS Lambda now supports Java 8, Java 11, and Java 17 runtimes on Amazon Linux 2023 (AL2023), available as both managed runtimes and container base images. These new runtimes enable customers running Lambda functions on Java 8, 11, or 17 to migrate from Amazon Linux 2 (AL2) to AL2023 without requiring a simultaneous Java version upgrade. The existing Lambda runtimes for Java 8, 11 and 17 run on AL2, which reached end of life on June 30, 2026. To maintain support coverage and SLA eligibility, customers must migrate their functions to an AL2023-based runtime. AWS recommends that customers upgrade to Java 21 or Java 25 on AL2023 as the preferred migration path. These runtimes offer the latest language features and performance improvements. For customers who are not yet ready to upgrade their Java version, the new Java 8, 11, and 17 runtimes on AL2023 provide an alternative forward path. In addition, the existing AL2-based Lambda runtimes for Java 8, 11, and 17 will remain supported and continue to receive patches for critical and selected important security issues until June 30, 2027, giving customers a full year after AL2's end of life to complete their migration. The Java 8, 11, and 17 runtimes on AL2023 are available in all AWS Regions where Lambda is available, including the AWS GovCloud (US) Regions and the China Regions. To learn more about AL2023 support in Lambda, see our blog post . For customers ready to upgrade to Java 21 or Java 25, you can use AWS Transform custom to assist with the migration. To learn more about Lambda runtimes, visit the Lambda runtimes documentation .

title: Cars and Self-Image

body_text: Before I get into this, let me say that I despise stereotyping in just about any form. Most of us are far more complicated than a cheap soundbite about a single thing. I’m a guy who stubbornly holds onto the 30-year-old AOL email address through which I centralize automotive-related email traffic precisely because it’s my way of saying “If you think you know something about me because of the stereotype that all remaining AOL users are blue-haired old ladies with Jitterbug phones, the joke’s on you. ” However, there’s no getting around the fact that the cars we choose to drive (or abjectly refuse to be caught dead in) project something about who we are, whether we want them to or not. The late folk musician Bill Morrissey has a song called “ Car and driver ” in which he cleverly serves up some of these common stereotypes (“My BMW draws applause / I am not bound by traffic laws / my Volvo wagon will seat six / it’ll run on diesel or trail mix / I’ll bet you a ten, even a fiver / you find the car, I’ll find the driver / It really ain’t no big deal / to know who’s inside that automobile”). Though that’s funny, I’d like to try to steer (heh) clear of the usual stereotypes of who is or isn’t driving Subarus and Corvettes and why I’m highly unlikely to ever own either vehicle (well, maybe a tastefully pinstriped C3 Corvette ), but let’s just say that there is no universe in which I’m ever going to be driving a Tesla Cybertruck. For both daily drivers and pampered passion vehicles, we are nothing without our deeply held automotive opinions. Actually, I take that back. Let’s attack the BMW-driving stereotype head-on. I’ve daily-driven BMWs for nearly 45 years, not because of their advertising as “The Ultimate Driving Machine” for the affluent, and in spite of the longstanding bad image they’ve had for being piloted by hostile drivers. This all began in the yuppie years when the cars were known for having their high beams on at all hours (a problem perpetuated by BMW’s own advertising that frequently showed the cars with all their candlepower blazing), morphed into ridicule of people who didn’t know how to use their directionals, and (as per Morrissey’s lyrics) settled into the aggressive tailgating “a$$hole in a BMW” who tries to weave through dense traffic at triple-digit speeds. (Honestly, this behavior used to seem limited to BMWs, Porsches, and Corvettes, but now I see Priuses and hooptie minivans doing it. I hate it having become so ubiquitous—it’s dangerous as hell—but at least it takes the spotlight off BMW.) As I’ve written, my daily driver for the past decade has been a 2003 BMW E39 530i with a 5-speed manual and the sport package. To me and others, this generation represents not only “peak BMW” but also the water’s edge of cars I want to own. The E39 doesn’t have those gawd-awful huge front kidneys (a friend of mine commented that “they look like the impression it would make if a fat naked guy fell butt-first into the snow” and now I can’t unsee it). I’ve read where people refer to the E39 as an “analog car,” and that’s ludicrous considering that it has 20 to 30 control modules depending on the option package. But at least it has no badly integrated diagnostic display that looks like someone ordered it from Temu, bolted it to the dashboard, and used 3D-shaded icons from Windows 3.1. It’s rear-wheel drive, so there are no front CV joints to need replacing. It’s got an old-school, mechanically driven water pump, not an electric one that requires pulling half the nose off to replace. It doesn’t have electrically assisted steering. And it’s now old enough that it’s an event when I see another one on the road. I’ve kept the E39 for a decade because, to me, it’s the perfect daily driver. With its 230-hp, 24-valve inline six, it has exactly the right amount of power to move the car out of its own way but not so much that you keep goosing it just for the rush. The suspension is firm but not in the least bit jarring. It’s a very comfortable, quiet car with a great stereo. I can cruise at the 80-mph traffic speeds you routinely encounter on interstates and average about 25 mpg. It’s got fold-down rear seats, allowing me to slide things into the trunk that I couldn’t otherwise. And it’s not a “look-at-me” car. In fact, it’s almost invisible, except to other E39 owners. A friend of mine recently sent me a link to a video titled “The psychology of people who still love old BMWs.” It’s obviously AI-generated, so the curmudgeon in me doesn’t want to include the link, but it actually does a decent job of hitting on many of the issues of engagement and ownership commitment that I and others love about older cars. And, incredibly, the video’s thumbnail picture shows a silver E39 just like mine. Of course, the last thing I want is to be part of some trend. I don’t want the cars I love to become “hot.” I want them to be undiscovered treasures, like empty beaches you can only reach by driving a slightly-lifted old Suburban through bogs thick with mosquitoes. But it does raise this issue of daily-driving “mature” cars. Between doing what most people do—daily-driving a sub-four-year-old, sub-60,000-mile, leased car—and trying to daily a beloved classic (which I really don’t recommend, but hey, you do you), there is a vast gray area. My E39 530i is now a 23-year-old car with 225,000 miles on it, but as long as I address any fuel delivery issues (new fuel pump and filter), ignition issues (replacing the stuck coils when they begin misfiring), cooling system issues (keeping after the water pump, radiator, thermostat, fan, clutch, and hoses), and charging system issues (alternator and regulator), it’s a safe and generally reliable modern car. Still, keeping a “mature” car that way is a commitment, and the people I know who do it (including me) justify it to themselves with a heady mix of iconoclastic bravado, economic calculus, and outright denial. I have several good friends who are joined at the hip with station wagons. One is on his fourth BMW E46 wagon, which are difficult but not impossible to find in a manual-transmission, rear-wheel drive configuration. Another loves the 1979–1985 Mercedes W123-chassis 300TD wagon, all of which were rear-wheel drive automatics. A third continues to be hooked on Volvo 245 RWD wagons built from 1975 through 1993, many of which were sticks. Part of the justification is that—particularly with the Mercedes and the Volvo—they’re fairly simple vehicles. But they’re also right-sized, satisfying to drive, and not some interchangeably-styled crossover SUV whose manufacturer you probably couldn’t tell if the badge was removed. And yet, if you’re driving a mature or classic vehicle, there’s no denying that you’re driving around a statement that says “This car is more important to me than the convenience of having something newer and blander.” Whether there’s also a component that’s “ BEING SEEN IN THIS CAR MAKING THIS STATEMENT is more important to me,” and if so, whether or not you care, is for the owner to decide. (That having been said, I saw a post on a vintage Lotus site where someone asked what the logistics would be about daily driving a Lotus Europa in Manhattan. While I’m all for letting that automotive freak flag fly, my visceral reaction was “Dude, there’s a line, and this is waaaay over it.”) I believe I’ve told this story before, but two cars before I had my current E39 530i, I had a BMW E39 wagon as a daily. Cool car, 5-speed, sport package, slightly hunkered-down suspension. But it was always breaking. In the end, I realized that my daily had the needs of an enthusiast car and thus could no longer function as my daily, and I didn’t want it as an enthusiast car, so I sold it. It wasn’t a difficult decision. I never regretted it. The car was never part of my self-image. I never thought of myself as “that guy daily-driving the BMW wagon” in the same way I think of myself as “that guy who’s owned his red BMW 3.0CSi for 40 years, has owned forty 2002s, and adores his two vintage Lotuses.” When the 530i gets too needy to be a daily and the time comes to cut it loose, I’ll be sad, but just as practical. It’s your choice. If your self-image has you daily-driving a Fiero up to 200,000 miles like Marshall in How I Met Your Mother, I salute you. And if you reach the point where that makes no sense and you and your spouse think you need some new generic crossover SUV—hey, you fought the good fight as long as you could. Someone else on the left edge of that bell curve will be thrilled to buy it and see themselves driving something unconventional. Maybe a few years later, you’ll see them on the road, livin’ their dream, and think, “Look at that peacock. Look at that gadfly. Ha! I mock you, sir! I give him another six months until he grows up and buys a Kia Seltos.” Which you utter, with a deep sense of self-loathing and shame, from behind the wheel of your Subaru Forester. *** Rob’s newly expanded book, The Best of The Hack Mechanic: 40 years of hacks, kluges, and assorted automotive mayhem , is available on Amazon here .
